tur19-0: Often yes, but with a reduced load. If the pain while running stays mild and is no worse the next morning, you can carry on. Cut back on hills, tempo runs and speed sessions for a while. In a randomised trial of 38 patients, those who kept running and jumping while monitoring their pain recovered just as well on the same exercise programme as those who stopped these activities for the first 6 weeks; continuing activity showed no harmful effect.
tur19-1: In a Norwegian study of 554 people aged 18–60, non-surgical treatment, open surgery and minimally invasive surgery gave similar results after one year. The tendon re-ruptured in 6.2% of the non-surgical group and 0.6% of the surgical groups; nerve injury occurred in 0.6% of the non-surgical group, 2.8% after open surgery and 5.2% after minimally invasive surgery. Surgery is considered more often for late presentation (more than 2–3 weeks), re-rupture, the tendon pulling away from the bone and elite athletes. In a 2019 meta-analysis pooling 29 studies, surgery also meant fewer re-ruptures but more of other complications; in studies using early-movement (functional) rehabilitation, the re-rupture rate did not differ between the two groups. The decision is made with your doctor. For non-surgical treatment, the UKSTAR trial of 540 people in the UK found that a walking boot allowing immediate weight-bearing gave similar results to a plaster cast: function scores at 9 months did not differ, and re-rupture occurred in 5% of those treated with a boot and 6% of those treated with a cast.
tur19-2: If your balance, muscle strength and sense of where your ankle is have not fully recovered after a sprain, the ankle becomes prone to spraining again. The way to break this cycle is to keep doing balance and strengthening exercises even after the pain has gone, and to return to sport gradually. A meta-analysis combining 4 studies in football players found that a structured warm-up programme done regularly before training (FIFA 11+) reduced ankle injuries by 32%.
tur19-3: It depends on your job. The NHS says usually 4–6 weeks; according to one NHS leaflet, you may return to desk work after 6–8 weeks and to heavy manual work after at least 3 months, sometimes 6. Decide with your surgeon. In an older study (1999) that followed 152 people given no activity restrictions after surgery, 98% returned to work, with an average of 1.2 weeks off work; returning early was not linked to re-herniation or repeat surgery. This was an observational study without a comparison group.

The American Academy of Pain Medicine's 2026 guideline also recommends against routine early imaging and against opioids as first-line treatment for low back pain lasting less than 6 weeks, with or without pain spreading to the leg, when there are no signs of serious disease.

tur19-16: According to a Cochrane review updated in 2026, exercise slightly improves pain and function in hip osteoarthritis; the average effect is small. Even so, because it has few side effects and many benefits for your overall health, the American College of Rheumatology strongly recommends exercise. Exercise is one part of a treatment package, together with weight control, a walking stick and understanding the condition properly. The UK’s 2022 guideline (NICE) likewise recommends exercise tailored to the person for everyone, weight loss for those who are overweight (even a small amount of weight loss helps) and a walking stick if needed; it states that imaging is usually not needed for diagnosis and that glucosamine and strong opioids are not recommended. An umbrella review published in 2026, bringing together 5 systematic reviews and 28 randomised trials, also found the effect of exercise on hip pain to be negligible; the authors recommend shared decision-making that does not overlook the general health benefits of exercise or patients' preferences.

tur19-18: Yes. A Cochrane review of 40 studies showed that exercises focused on walking, balance and everyday tasks after leaving hospital clearly improve mobility. In a US study of 232 patients, a 6-month home exercise programme improved function further, even in patients who had already completed rehabilitation. Not every programme is equally effective: in the CAP trial of 210 patients, at the end of a 16-week home programme the proportion reaching the threshold for independent walking in the community (more than 300 metres in 6 minutes) was 23% in the group doing aerobic, strength and balance exercise and 18% in the group receiving range-of-motion exercises and electrical nerve stimulation. The difference was not significant, but walking improved markedly in both groups.
tur19-19: In the review of 24 trials (3,046 people), home programmes supported by healthcare staff and centre-based programmes were found to be similarly effective. Choose the one you will be able to keep up regularly; a home programme also needs a doctor’s approval and regular follow-up. According to the UK’s national audit of cardiac rehabilitation, about 70–80% of people who start a programme complete it; the NHS aims for 85% of people who have had a heart attack to take part. In a US study that followed 1,120 people referred for cardiac rehabilitation for about 4 years, the death rate was 12% among those who took part in a home-based programme and 20% among those who did not; as this was an observational study, other factors may also have played a role.

If that target feels far away, start with shorter sessions; a little movement is better than none. In a 2026 meta-analysis of 21 randomised trials and 8,449 patients, those taking part in structured exercise programmes had a 23% lower likelihood of death and a 17% lower likelihood of recurrence; aerobic exercise alone or combined with strength exercise was linked to better survival.

tur19-29: It can. In a combined analysis of studies, about 39% of shoulders that had dislocated forwards for the first time dislocated again or slipped out of place. Being aged 40 or under, being male and having naturally loose joints increase this chance. Physiotherapy strengthens the shoulder muscles; in younger people and after repeated dislocations, surgery may also be discussed. A 2018 analysis combining 22 randomised trials found that about 47% of those managed without surgery after a first dislocation had no further dislocation within 2 years. Holding the arm turned outwards in a special brace did not reduce redislocation; the authors consider an ordinary arm sling for comfort to be sufficient.
tur19-30: The first step is controlling the pain and keeping the arm moving as far as the pain allows. If the pain does not settle, your doctor may suggest a steroid injection, breaking up and washing out the calcium with a needle under ultrasound guidance (lavage), or shockwave therapy. A review found that lavage may be more effective than shockwave therapy or a steroid injection alone, but the quality of the evidence is low. Surgery is kept for the rare cases where pain cannot be controlled in other ways. In a randomised trial of 48 patients whose pain persisted despite other treatments, those who had lavage plus a steroid injection had improved more after 1 year than those who had a steroid injection alone, and the risk of complications was low.
